docs.text: Beneath the Mesa Assessing Aquifer, Well, and Acequia Water Resources Across Sandoval County, New Mexico ENG 220 · Team 23 Open the live app · View the code on GitHub About the project Water scarcity is a persistent challenge across New Mexico. Sandoval County spans several hydrogeologic settings, and its communities depend on a mix of groundwater wells, surface water, and acequia irrigation systems. This project evaluates the condition and long-term viability of those water resources across the county, with Cuba, New Mexico, on the eastern edge of the San Juan Basin, as a focused case study. The project is motivated by concern about declining groundwater near Cuba, but rather than assume how severe that decline is or what is causing it, we test what the available public data actually show. Approach The study works at two levels: County-wide screening. Map and compare aquifers, wells, water levels, water quality, and acequia and surface-water features across Sandoval County. Because the county crosses several geologic regions, comparisons are grouped by region or aquifer system instead of treating the county as one uniform aquifer. Cuba case study. A closer look at the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation near Cuba, using San Juan Basin aquifer datasets alongside nearby well, water-level, and water-quality records. The analysis focuses on measurable indicators such as depth to water, water-level change over time, well depth, aquifer unit, and salinity, rather than a full hydrologic model. Where records are sparse, the results say so instead of filling the gaps. Research questions How do groundwater levels vary across Sandoval County, and which areas show sustained decline, stability, or recovery? What do well records show about well depth, depth to water, and the aquifer units that communities rely on? Do the available data support the concern that Cuba's main groundwater source is approaching severe depletion? How do the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation compare near Cuba in extent, thickness, hydraulic properties, water levels, and water quality? How does groundwater quality, including salinity, vary across the county and near Cuba? Where are acequias located, what surface water do they depend on, and which communities do they serve? Do changes in groundwater levels line up with nearby surface-water or acequia conditions, or are the records too limited to tell? Where is monitoring coverage strong, and where are the most important data gaps? Which indicators can be combined into a dashboard that shows water-resource stress without overstating how certain the data are? How this site is organized The site follows the project's stages, from collecting data to presenting results. Each stage page explains what was done, which files it produced, and who led it. docs.text: 2. Data cleaning Lead: James Wanueka This stage turns the raw downloads into tables the analysis code can use directly. Cleaning makes the data correct and consistent; it doesn't draw conclusions. Averaging, trends, and narrowing to the Cuba area happen in the analysis stage. Where files go What Where Example Raw downloads (never edited) data/ data/ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv Cleaning scripts cleaning/ cleaning/clean_aquifer_tests.py Cleaned files data/clean/ data/clean/aquifer_tests.csv Each cleaned file has a script with a matching name that reads the raw file and writes the cleaned one, so anyone can rerun it and get the same result. Python or MATLAB both work. If a step is done by hand in Excel, write it down under Cleaning steps . Conventions for cleaned files Every cleaned file follows the same rules, so the files can be combined and charted the same way. File names: lowercase with underscores, describing what's inside, such as groundwater_levels_monthly.csv . No dates, versions, or "final" in names; GitHub keeps the history. Column names: lowercase with underscores, with the unit at the end, such as well_depth_ft or transmissivity_drawdown_ft2_per_day . Shared columns: every file starts with these, using the same names: Column Contents site_id The source's ID for the well or site, as text site_name The well or site name latitude , longitude Decimal degrees date YYYY-MM-DD source Where the data came from, such as USGS or NM OSE Rows: one row per measurement, sorted by site_id and then date . Values: Numbers only, with no units, commas, or ranges inside cells. Missing values left blank. Never use 0 , N/A , or -9999 , which charts would plot as real values. Dates as YYYY-MM-DD . Text trimmed of extra spaces and spelled consistently. File format: comma-separated, UTF-8, one header row, and no index column. In pandas, use df.to_csv(path, index=False) . From Excel, save as "CSV UTF-8". What to keep: IDs, location, date, and every measurement the analysis might use. Drop columns that are empty or identical in every row. What each raw file needs Groundwater levels → data/clean/groundwater_levels_monthly.csv From data/water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv : Keep groundwater-level rows only: parameter_code 72019. Keep one period and statistic: interval_type is month and parent_statistic_name is Mean . That leaves 2,673 rows for 9 wells, with no duplicates. Rename to the shared columns: monitoring_location_id → site_id , monitoring_location_name → site_name , y → latitude , x → longitude , start_date → date , and arithmetic_mean → depth_to_water_ft . Set source to USGS . Keep wells with an A or B suffix as separate sites. They're measured at different depths at the same location, so don't average them together. Values are depth below land surface, so a larger number means a lower water table. The other measurements in this file (streamflow, reservoir storage, water quality) can follow the same pattern later, one file per measurement. Aquifer tests → data/clean/aquifer_tests.csv From data/ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv : Keep Sandoval County only: COUNTY NAME is SANDOVAL , which leaves 179 rows. The file starts with a hidden byte-order mark, so the first column name can appear as ï»¿ObjectID . In pandas, read the file with encoding="utf-8-sig" . Keep one row per test. The same well ( OSE POD ID ) can appear more than once, so don't remove rows just because a well ID repeats. Convert dates such as 11/12/2002 12:00:00 AM to 2002-11-12 . START WATER LEVEL DATE uses 1/1/1900 when the date is unknown. Leave those blank. Some numbers are stored as text, and one hydraulic conductivity value is a range ( 11 to 21 ). Convert everything to numbers, decide how to handle ranges, and record the decision under Problems and decisions . Fix misspelled formation names and extra spaces, such as POINT LOOKOUT SAANDSTONE and MENEFEE FORMATION . Drop empty and administrative columns. GROUND SURFACE ELEVATION - FT AMSL is blank for every Sandoval row, and columns such as GlobalID , Entered By , Creator , and Editor aren't needed. Some test dates are January 1, which may mean only the year is known. Keep them, but note it. Suggested columns, in order: site_id (from OSE POD ID ), site_name ( ALT WELL NAME ), latitude , longitude , date (test start), source ( NM OSE ), formation , well_depth_ft , screen_top_ft , screen_bottom_ft , depth_to_water_ft (start water level), pumping_rate_gpm , transmissivity_drawdown_ft2_per_day , transmissivity_recovery_ft2_per_day , storativity , specific_capacity_gpm_per_ft , and hydraulic_conductivity_ft_per_day . Cleaning steps To be written: each step, in order, and the script that does it. Cleaned outputs To be written: each cleaned file, its row count, and the script that makes it. Problems and decisions To be written: missing values, odd records, and how they were handled.

docs.text: 1. Data collection Lead: Dylan Gonzales This stage covers finding public datasets that can answer the research questions , downloading them, and recording where each one comes from. Datasets in the repository water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv USGS monthly and yearly statistics for 30 monitoring sites in Sandoval County (17 stream gages, 9 wells, 2 canals, and 2 reservoirs), with records from 1926 to 2026. Covers streamflow, depth to groundwater, reservoir storage, suspended sediment, water temperature, and water-quality measures: specific conductance, dissolved oxygen, pH, and turbidity. Source: To be added: link to the page this file was downloaded from. ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv New Mexico Office of the State Engineer aquifer-test records, 3,455 statewide and 179 in Sandoval County, including well depth, screened interval, geologic formation, and hydraulic properties such as transmissivity and storativity. Source: To be added: link to the page this file was downloaded from. Why these datasets To be written: why each dataset was chosen and which research questions it helps answer. Still to collect The proposal also calls for the following data, which isn't in the repository yet: Aquifer geometry near Cuba: USGS San Juan Basin digital aquifer data for the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation. Water quality and salinity: the NM Bureau of Geology San Juan Basin Brackish Water Assessment and New Mexico Water Data records. Acequias: locations and service areas of acequias and community ditches from the NM Interstate Stream Commission. More water-level records: National Ground-Water Monitoring Network and Healy Collaborative Groundwater Monitoring Network data, to add wells beyond the 9 in the USGS file. Shallow groundwater depth: the mean annual depth to groundwater for the shallow riparian aquifer dataset. County boundary: a Sandoval County boundary layer to organize the maps. Sources USGS San Juan Basin digital aquifer data (ScienceBase) USGS groundwater-flow model report, WRI 95-4187 NM Bureau of Geology: San Juan Basin Brackish Water Assessment New Mexico Office of the State Engineer National Ground-Water Monitoring Network Healy Collaborative Groundwater Monitoring Network New Mexico Water Data Catalog NM Interstate Stream Commission: Acequias
